title: MB7-26181
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The Appellants, a married couple, XXXX XXXX (the Husband) and XXXX XXXX (the Wife), citizens of India, appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated December 5, 2017, rejecting their claims for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The Appellants, a married couple, XXXX XXXX (the Husband) and XXXX XXXX (the Wife), citizens of India, appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated December 5, 2017, rejecting their claims for refugee protection. The Appellants fear the Punjab police who allege that they are linked to militants through the Husband's brother. The RPD found that the Appellants have a viable internal flight alternative (IFA) in Delhi or Mumbai. I have reviewed the record, the testimony and arguments of the Appellants, and I agree with the RPD that the Appellants have a viable IFA in Delhi or Mumbai. The appeal is dismissed.

According to their Basis of Claim Forms (BOCs),1 the Appellants are Sikh and were both born in 1981 in villages approximately 5 km apart in the Amritsar district of Punjab state. The Husband worked on the XXXX XXXX and the Wife is a XXXX.

In June 2006 and December 2006, the police arrested and tortured the Husband's brother, XXXX, alleging he was involved with militants. The Husband, with the help of an agent, sent XXXX to live in England. On November 14, 2014, British authorities returned XXXX to India. In August 2015 and September 2016, the police arrested XXXX alleging that he was involved with drug smugglers and terrorists, he participated in terrorist meetings while in England, and returned to organize terrorism attacks in India. After his second arrest, XXXX was released on condition that he report to the police each month. Afraid of the police, the Husband sent XXXX to live with relatives in Haryana. When XXXX failed to report to the police on November 1, 2016, they began looking for him, alleging that he had joined the militants.

On January 14, 2017, while the Wife's brother XXXX was visiting the Appellants, the police raided the Appellants' farm because they had received information that XXXX and other militants were present. The police conducted a search and arrested the Husband and XXXX. The police tortured the Husband who revealed the whereabouts of his brother XXXX. The police went to Haryana to arrest XXXX, but he managed to elude the police and to date his whereabouts remain unknown. On January 15 and 17, 2017, respectively, the police released XXXX and the Husband from detention. XXXX died on January 25, 2017 from the injuries he suffered from being tortured in detention.

The Appellants decided to leave India with their children and retained the services of an agent. On February 14, 2017, XXXX father visited the Appellants with a lawyer asking the Husband to be a witness for a complaint against the police. On February 16, 2017, the police raided the Appellants' home; the Husband was absent, but the police told his children to tell him to report to the police station. The police arrested the Wife, detained her for one night and subjected her to physical and sexual abuse. The Wife was released following payment of a bribe and after she promised not to proceed with a complaint against the police or disclose the sexual assault.

The Husband moved to Delhi with the agent, and the Wife and their children followed in the first week of XXXX 2017. While the agent was able to arrange Canadian visas for the Appellants, he was not able to obtain visas for their children. The Appellants arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2017. The police continue to ask about the Appellants and allege that they have joined the militants.
The Appellants filed refugee claims on July 17, 2017, which were heard on September 12, 2017. The RPD made its decision on December 5, 2017.

The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) reviews decisions of the RPD on a standard of correctness after conducting an independent assessment of the evidence before it. The exception to this rule is where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in assessing and weighing the oral testimony heard, which in particular cases attracts deference.2 Unless specifically stated below, I have applied the correctness standard.
The determinative issue on this appeal is whether or not the RPD was correct in finding that the Appellants have a viable IFA in Mumbai or Delhi. IFA test

The test for assessing an IFA is two-pronged and is set out in the Federal Court of Appeal decision in Rasaratnam:3 (1) The Board must be satisfied on a balance of probabilities that there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted in the part of the country to which it finds an IFA exists and/or the claimant would not be personally subject to a risk to life or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture in the IFA. (2) Moreover, the conditions in the part of the country considered to be an IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claim, for him to seek refuge there.

Both prongs must be satisfied to find that a claimant has an IFA. Once the issue of IFA has been raised and potential IFAs identified, the burden of proof rests with the claimants to show that they do not have an IFA. The finding of an IFA must be based on a distinct evaluation of the region for that purpose, taking into account the claimants' personal circumstances. An IFA must be a realistic and attainable option. The claimants cannot be required to encounter great physical danger or undergo undue hardship in travelling to an IFA and staying there. RPD IFA findings

The RPD complied with the procedural requirements to raise an IFA before or during the hearing. The potential IFAs in Mumbai and Delhi were canvassed with the Appellants at the RPD hearing on September 12, 2017.4
The RPD correctly identified the two-prong IFA test.5

The RPD found that the Appellants do not have a well-founded fear of persecution and do not, on a balance of probabilities, face harm in Mumbai or Delhi. In arriving at this decision, the RPD considered whether the Punjab police would learn of the Appellants' presence in the proposed IFAs and whether the police in Mumbai or Delhi would take a significant interest in the Appellants' case.

The RPD provided the Appellants with the opportunity to describe the difficulties they would face living in Delhi or Mumbai. The Appellants stated that they are not well-educated and only speak Punjabi. The husband indicated that he has worked exclusively in farming and the wife has only worked as a homemaker. Following its assessment, the RPD concluded that the Appellant's relocation to the proposed IFAs would not be unreasonable. Appellant's IFA submissions

The Appellant argues that the RPD's IFA conclusion was manifestly unreasonable in the circumstances,6 and its analysis was made in a factual vacuum or, at least, on a mistaken premise,7 specifically: * The Appellants presented evidence that the police have the willingness and capacity to find them, which was ignored by the RPD;8 * In a situation where people are suspected of militant activity, as in the case of the Appellants, it is unlikely that the police communicate publicly with other police forces due to investigation secrecy requirements;9 * Notwithstanding the objective evidence cited by the RPD in its decision about the lack of communication and collaboration of Indian police, the contrary evidence cited by the Appellants is more relevant;10 * Mumbai and/or Delhi would be a nightmare for the Appellants-Sikh farmers with little education-who do not fit the professional or religious profile11 and do not speak the local language;12 * The RPD recognizes the existence of a tenant verification procedure throughout India, which means that the Punjab police can easily find the Appellant in the IFAs;13 * Delhi borders on Punjab, is a megalopolis with more than 16 million inhabitants and virtually no arable land, and Mumbai is the financial centre of India where agricultural activity is also problematic due to a lack of land. The Appellants argue that they would always be subject to systemic discrimination because they are not native to either IFA.14

The Appellant concludes that the RPD's decision is not reasonable, because it is unintelligible and unacceptable as an outcome that can be justified in light of the facts and the law.15 RAD IFA analysis First prong-no serious possibility of persecution or risk of harm

The RPD found that there was no serious possibility of persecution or risk of harm to the Appellants in Mumbai or Delhi based on whether the Punjab police would learn of the Appellants' presence in the proposed IFAs and whether the Mumbai or Delhi police would take a significant interest in the Appellants' case.

When the RPD proposed relocation, the Husband testified that wherever they go in India, they will have to provide proof of their identity. According to the Appellants, the police in any IFA would contact the police in their area, who would say that they are looking for them and ask for the Appellants to be handed over to the Punjab police.16

The RPD surveyed the objective evidence and reported the following in its reasons: * Some cities have laws which require house owners to register tenants with local authorities. The police in Mumbai indicate that they conduct regular tenant verification;17 * Sources state that there are no written procedures about how police verify tenant information. This can include cross-referencing with lists of wanted persons. Police may perform background checks, but this practice is irregular. Records are checked and cross-checked only in cases of serious incidents of crime;18 * A source quoted in a Response to Information Request (RIR) dated May 10, 2016, states that police stations across India are "virtually unconnected islands" in terms of tracking crime and criminals. Indian police have no system for effectively storing, sharing or accessing dates, and police units have no system for communicating with each other except for major cases like terrorism or high-profile organized crime;19 * Other documentary evidence referenced by the Appellants' counsel during submissions, RIRs dated May 14, 2012 and May 13, 2013, state that police forces in India can communicate through informal means20 and with police stations in different states to find persons of interest.21

The RPD found that the Appellants had not presented any evidence that: they face formal charges; face arrest warrants for serious crimes; the police have issued a first information report against them; or the Punjab police have informed federal authorities that they are suspected of militant involvement. The RPD observed that the Appellants exited India using their own genuine passports and did not describe any efforts to circumvent airport security.

The RPD concluded that the Appellants had not demonstrated that the Punjab police consider them implicated in an extreme case involving serious crime and would seek cooperation with other police forces, or that their names appears on a list of persons of interest available to the police in Mumbai or Delhi.
The Appellants argue that they presented evidence that the Punjab police have the willingness and capacity to find them but they do not reference any specific evidence in their submissions.

The Appellants argue that where a person is suspected of militant activity, as in their case, it is unlikely that the police communicate publicly with other police forces due to investigation secrecy requirements. The Appellants do not support this argument with reference to any evidence. My review of the objective evidence suggests that the opposite is true and that there is a national system for police cooperation on terrorism.22 There are two agencies operating under the Ministry of Home Affairs: the Central Bureau of Investigation, which deals with economic crimes and serious non-economic crimes including terrorism; and the National Investigation Agency established in 2008 to investigate terrorist activity and other criminal offences related to national security.23

The Appellants argue that the 2016 RIR24 cited by the RPD to support its finding that there is little interstate police communication and collaboration is refuted by the evidence they provided, but they do not reference the objective evidence in their submissions. I assume that the Appellants' evidence is the RIRs dated May 14, 201225 and May 13, 201326 which were cited in their counsel's submissions to the RPD and referenced in the RPD decision. The RPD clearly addresses why it prefers the information in the 2016 RIR. The RPD says that the 2016 RIR is more recent, the 2012 RIR emphasizes the need for collaboration, and the 2013 RIR reiterates that the Punjab police would only track someone to another state in extreme circumstances.27

I recognize that the objective evidence about police communication is not consistent. I have reviewed the most recent objective evidence,28 an RIR dated June 25, 2018, which says that the only police database that exists in India is the Crime and Criminal Tracking Network and Systems (CCTNS), "a database with information on crime and criminals that interconnects police stations across the country."29 There is not much specific information on categories of persons that may be included in police databases. The objective evidence says that "tracking of persons of interest is difficult and police have a mixed record of success."30 According to one source: [i]f they put their minds to it, police authorities in India are able to track and locate persons of interest, depending on the heinousness of the crime and the pressure received from political authorities. For example, it is possible [for them] to locate a person of interest in cases of rape, murder or armed robbery. Social class also plays a vital role: the likelihood of prosecution is much greater if a case involves the murder of a politician's daughter versus the murder of a slum dweller.31

The same recent objective evidence32 does not support a finding that a tenant verification of the Appellants would result in the Punjab police being contacted. The objective evidence cites a Mumbai police commissioner who stated: "it is impossible for the police to actually verify the identity of all those who rent property...the police force is not equipped to personally go and check all new tenants..."33 Another source cited by the objective evidence says that "the police is just ill-equipped and short-staffed to actually carry out such verifications when they get over 50 forms daily."34

The Appellants' evidence is that they travelled to Canada from Delhi using their own passports, which were issued in 2014 and 2016 to the Husband and Wife, respectively. The objective evidence35 indicates that at the international airport in Delhi,36 the Appellants would have undergone an immigration check by the Bureau of Immigration (BOI). The BOI reports that Indian nationals must fill a departure card at the time of departure, including their name, date of birth, passport number, and address in India. Air India states that "embarkation forms should be duly filled out and submitted to customs and immigration authorities before boarding the aircraft."37 The objective evidence identifies four components to the immigration check: checking of passport/travel documents to identify the holder and to look out for cases of forgery; ascertain the eligibility of the holder either to leave or enter India, as per existing rules and regulations; computer confirmation in clearing passengers; and a health check.38 I find that the Appellants would have been required to provide the required documentation, undergo an immigration check by the Indian immigration authorities prior to boarding their aircraft, and would have been stopped if their names were in a police database or on a list of wanted persons.

The Appellants have not been charged or convicted of any crime,39 first information reports were not filed, and they are not in a police database or on a list of wanted persons. For the reasons cited by the RPD, as supported by the most recent objective evidence, I find that if the Appellants' names were verified as part of any identity verification process, it would not, on a balance of probabilities, cause the Delhi or Mumbai police to alert the Punjab police or cause the Punjab police to have an interest in pursuing the Appellants in Delhi or Mumbai. I agree with the RPD that the Appellant does not have a well-founded fear of persecution and does not, on a balance of probabilities, face harm in Mumbai or Delhi. The first prong of the IFA test is met. Second prong-not objectively unreasonable (or unduly harsh) in the circumstances

When the RPD asked the Husband at the hearing what would happen if he relocated to Delhi or Mumbai, he identified the following issues: (a) he is not well educated; (b) he only speaks Punjabi; and (c) he only knows farming.40 When the RPD asked the Wife the same question, she said that she is only willing to live in Punjab and do her housework. She also said that she was not very well educated and does not speak any language other than Punjabi.41 Following its assessment, the RPD concluded that the Appellants' relocation to the proposed IFAs would not be unreasonable.

The Appellants argue that Mumbai and/or Delhi would be a nightmare for them because they are XXXX XXXX with little education who do not speak the local language and who do not fit the professional or religious profile. The Appellants argue that Delhi borders on Punjab state and that neither Delhi nor Mumbai has much arable land or agricultural activity.

The Federal Court has set a high threshold when determining whether a proposed IFA is unreasonable or unduly harsh: the onus is on the Appellants to show that it would be "objectively unreasonable."42

The Appellants are both 38 years old and neither presented any evidence of physical or psychological impediment to their seeking gainful employment. In their generic immigration application, both Appellants report 10 years of education and that their intended occupation is "general work."43 I find that the Appellants have the basic skills to obtain employment in the IFAs.

Mumbai and Delhi are among the major urban areas of India, with populations in excess of 21 million and 25.7 million, respectively.44 The objective evidence45 cited by the RPD says that every major Indian city has a strong Sikh community.46 Several sources cited reveal that Sikh minorities living outside Punjab have access to housing, employment, health care, and education, and have the freedom to practise their religion.47

I have considered the Appellants' personal situation and the documentary evidence including the country conditions for Sikhs who relocate in India, and I agree with the RPD that the Appellants have failed to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that it would be unreasonable or result in undue hardship if they seek refuge in the proposed IFAs in Delhi or Mumbai. Therefore, the second prong of the IFA test is also met.

I have reviewed the evidence on the record, including the recording of the September 12, 2017 hearing, assessed the Appellants' submissions and considered the most recent objective evidence. Following my independent analysis, I find that the Appellants have an IFA in Mumbai or Delhi. I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that there is no serious possibility of the Appellants being persecuted in Mumbai or Delhi and that it would not be objectively unreasonable in all the circumstances for the Appellants to live there.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
